tagline.text: Eastern Samar's surf island, where Pacific swells first make landfall

location.label: Location
location.text: Guiuan, Eastern Samar (southeastern tip of Samar Island)

children.text: A long island linked by bridge to Guiuan at the southeastern tip of Samar Island, where unobstructed Pacific swells have earned it the nickname "Visayas' surfing capital." Quiet white-sand beaches, a forest lagoon, and the Magellan landing site at Homonhon, along with traces of World War II, all lie close by.

Calicoan Island belongs to Guiuan, Eastern Samar, stretching south in a thin strip from the southeastern tip of the Samar mainland. Its west side faces the calm waters of Leyte Gulf, while its east side faces the Philippine Sea and the open Pacific, letting you see two completely different seas on a single island. The island connects to downtown Guiuan by bridge, and the Guiuan–Sulangan road running the length of the island lets you drive all the way to Sulangan at the southern tip.

What made this island famous is the surf. Pacific swells break straight onto the coral reef along the east coast, forming one of the Philippines' finest reef breaks, and surf camps and resorts have sprung up around a spot travelers know as "ABCD Beach." In
September 2023
, a national surfing competition here earned it the nickname "Visayas' surfing capital." On smaller-wave days, beginner lessons are also available.
The forest in the island's interior holds six lagoons of various sizes, the largest reaching about
30ha

. Caves are scattered along the cliff edges, and Linao Cave on the island's south side is beloved as a cave pool filled with blue water. Seaweed and pearl farming take place in the surrounding waters too, giving the coast an endearing fishing-village feel.
The Guiuan area also has deep history. In
March 1521
, Magellan's expedition, having crossed the Pacific, made its first landfall in the Philippines at Homonhon Island, off Guiuan; in

, ahead of the Leyte landing, U.S. forces landed first on Suluan Island and then built a large naval base and airstrip in Guiuan. Guiuan was also the first place hit when Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) made landfall on
November 8, 2013
, though the town has steadily recovered since. This island is recommended for travelers who want empty beaches, waves, and a low-key fishing-village trip.

Calicoan's signature surf spot, with waves breaking over a coral reef. Experienced surfers should pick a day with a bigger swell, while beginners should try with an instructor on a smaller-wave day. Board rentals and lessons are available at the beach surf camps.

The east coast is one of the first places in the Philippines to see the sunrise. Watching the sun rise over the horizon along with the breaking waves early in the morning is the highlight of a trip to this island.
This cave, on the island's south side toward Sulangan, holds clear blue water inside for swimming. The steps and rocks are slippery, so wear sandals when entering.
The lagoons in the island's interior form wetlands home to birds, crabs, and small fish. They offer a quiet scene, different from the beaches, and are worth exploring on days when the surf is flat.

Built by Jesuits in the 18th century, this is one of the Philippines' most notable old churches, known for its shell decorations. It was heavily damaged by Typhoon Haiyan and has undergone ongoing restoration, and sits easy to visit beside the downtown plaza.

Homonhon Island, reached by boat from the Guiuan pier, holds a monument marking the 500th anniversary of Magellan's expedition's landing. It can be visited on a day trip that also takes in the island's beach and a waterfall.
At Calicoan's southern tip, the church of San Antonio in Sulangan is a major pilgrimage site in Eastern Samar. The coastal drive there is a scenic route in its own right.
The long airstrip the U.S. Navy built in Guiuan in 1944–1945 is still in use as an airport today. It offers a sense of just how important a supply base Guiuan was during the Battle of Leyte.

If you have an extra day, consider a boat trip from the Guiuan pier to Homonhon Island's Magellan landing monument and beach. Boat schedules change often depending on weather and sea conditions, so check at the pier the day before.
Fly into Tacloban Airport (TAC) from Manila or Cebu. From Manila it takes about
1 hour 15 minutes
, with one-way fares around
. Guiuan also has a long airstrip, but there are no scheduled passenger flights.
Chartering a private van from the airport to Guiuan takes about
3 to 3 hours 30 minutes
, at about
per vehicle.
Vans and buses bound for Guiuan depart frequently from Tacloban's New Bus Terminal from early morning through the afternoon. It's about
150km
, taking about
3–4 hours
, with fares around

Departures thin out later in the afternoon, so it's better to leave in the morning. If taking a long-distance bus across Samar from Manila, another route runs down through Borongan in Eastern Samar to Guiuan.
From the Guiuan terminal to accommodations on Calicoan Island is about
20–30 minutes
by tricycle or habal-habal (motorbike taxi), at about
. Some accommodations will arrange a pickup if you call ahead.
Nearby islands such as Homonhon and Suluan are reached by scheduled ferry or chartered outrigger boat from the integrated terminal pier in Guiuan. It takes about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes
to Homonhon, and boats don't run when the sea is rough.
For beaches and island travel,
March–June

, with relatively little rain and calm seas, is best. The water is also clearest on the eastern coast during this period, good for swimming and snorkeling, but the waves are small, so surfing is mostly limited to beginner lessons.
If surfing is your goal,
October–February
is considered the best window, when Pacific swell and the northeast monsoon reliably produce waves. Eastern Samar, though, is one of the rainiest regions in the Philippines, and
July–December

falls frequently in typhoon season, so check forecasts often and build slack into your schedule if traveling then. Wave conditions vary day to day, so checking with a local surf camp beforehand is the most reliable approach.

Lodging splits between surf resorts and guesthouses on Calicoan Island's east coast and small hotels in downtown Guiuan. To be close to the waves, accommodation on Calicoan near the surf spots is convenient — guesthouses run about
a night, and resorts with a pool about
. During peak season and surf competitions, rooms fill up fast, so book ahead. To save money, you can also stay in downtown Guiuan and commute by tricycle.

There aren't many restaurants on the island, so most meals are eaten at your accommodation's restaurant. Being a fishing area, freshly grilled fish, squid, crab, seaweed salad, and kinilaw are fresh and reasonably priced. Around Guiuan's market there are cheap local eateries and bakeries, and you can also buy Samar's specialty glutinous-rice snacks and coconut treats. Almost nothing on Calicoan stays open at night, so buy snacks and water in Guiuan beforehand.
Guiuan has ATMs, but they're few in number and often out of order. Bring plenty of cash from Tacloban.
Wind is light in the morning, keeping the wave faces clean. Surf right after sunrise or in the late afternoon for the best conditions.
Beginners can get hurt falling in the shallows over the reef, so always surf with an instructor, and wear aqua shoes or surf boots.
The sun is very strong, so wear a rash guard and reef-safe sunscreen.
Phone signal and internet can be weak in places, so check whether your accommodation has Wi-Fi beforehand.
Vans back to Tacloban thin out in the afternoon, so plan to leave in the morning on your last day.
If you're interested in history, look into the Leyte landing commemoration held around October 17 on Suluan Island.

Calicoan's east coast has strong waves and rip currents (fast currents pulling from shore out to sea). Avoid swimming near the surf spots, and beginners shouldn't go into the water alone on big-wave days.
It's a reef break with a sharp coral bottom. Surfing at low tide should be left to the judgment of experienced surfers and local instructors.
During typhoon season (
July–December
), flooded roads and suspended transport can occur, so check the weather forecast and local government notices.
Small island outrigger boats may not be able to return if the weather turns bad, so wear a life vest and don't set out if conditions look risky.
Some inland parts of Eastern Samar occasionally see safety advisories. Avoid traveling mountain roads late at night, and check the latest travel safety information.
The nearest major hospital is in Tacloban, so bring basic first-aid supplies and travel insurance in case of a surfing injury.
